A KVM (Keyboard, Video, Mouse) switch is a hardware device that typically allows a user to control multiple computers from a single set of peripherals (one keyboard, one monitor, and one mouse).

The Openterface Mini-KVM shown on your current page is a specific, portable type of "KVM-over-USB" solution designed for a different workflow:

  • How it works: Instead of switching a monitor between two towers, it turns your laptop into the KVM console. It connects a "target" computer (like a headless server, Raspberry Pi, or ATM) to your laptop via USB and HDMI.
  • What it does: It captures video and audio from the target device and sends it to an app on your laptop, allowing you to see the screen and control the mouse/keyboard input of the other device directly from your laptop window.
  • Key Benefit: Unlike remote desktop software, this hardware solution provides BIOS-level access, meaning you can control the target computer even if it crashes, has no OS installed, or isn't connected to the internet.

Based on the product page you are viewing, here is why someone would use this KVM and the details regarding its latency:

Why use a KVM?

The Openterface Mini-KVM is designed to help users control a computer without needing a separate monitor, keyboard, or mouse attached to it. It is particularly useful for:

  • Troubleshooting "Headless" Devices: It allows IT professionals to manage servers, Raspberry Pis, ATMs, or kiosks that don't have their own screens.
  • BIOS-Level Access: Unlike remote desktop software, this hardware solution lets you access a computer's BIOS or boot menu, which is critical if the operating system crashes or isn't installed yet.
  • Network Independence: It works without an internet connection, making it vital for fixing network issues or managing secure, air-gapped systems.
  • Portability: It replaces the need to carry bulky monitors and keyboards, turning your laptop into the console for other devices.

Is there latency?

Yes, there is a small amount of latency.

  • The specifications state the device has under 140 milliseconds of latency.
  • It supports video output up to 1920x1080 at 30Hz.

turns.prompt_text: I have a Mac Mini and a MacBook Air. My MacBook Mini has two monitors, and my MacBook Air I would sometimes wish to hook up so that I could use all three screens at the same time. Would a KVM help me with this, or would that be another item? https://www.crowdsupply.com/techxartisan/openterface-mini-kvm
turns.response_html:
Based on your description, the Openterface Mini-KVM shown on your screen is not the right tool for that specific goal.

Here is the breakdown of why, and what you likely need instead:

1. Why this specific KVM won't work

The Openterface Mini-KVM is designed for a different purpose: "Headless" control. It takes the video output from one computer (like a server or your Mac Mini) and displays it inside a window on your laptop screen. It does not let your MacBook Air take over the external monitors to create a three-screen setup.

2. What you likely need: A "Dual-Monitor KVM Switch"

To use your MacBook Air with the two external monitors (plus its own screen) and switch them back and forth with your Mac Mini, you need a Dual-Monitor KVM Switch.

  • How it works: You plug your keyboard, mouse, and both monitors into the KVM dock. Then, you connect both the Mac Mini and MacBook Air to the KVM.
  • The Result: You press a button to switch control. When switched to the MacBook Air, you would effectively have 3 screens (The Air's built-in screen + the 2 external monitors).

3. Important Caution: MacBook Air Limitations

Before buying a Dual-Monitor KVM, check your MacBook Air model:

  • M1 / M2 MacBook Air: These chips natively support only one external display. To use two external monitors, you would need a specialized "DisplayLink" dock/adapter, not just a simple KVM.
  • M3 MacBook Air: Supports two external displays, but only when the laptop lid is closed (meaning you would lose the third "laptop" screen).

4. Free Alternative: Universal Control

If your goal is simply to use both computers side-by-side without constantly switching cables, you might already have a solution built into macOS called Universal Control.

  • It allows you to use one keyboard and mouse to control both Macs wirelessly.
  • You can drag your mouse cursor from your Mac Mini's screens right over to your MacBook Air's screen as if they were one giant desktop, though they remain separate computers.

Based on your description, you do not need the "Openterface Mini-KVM" shown on your current screen. That device is for viewing a computer inside a window on another screen (like a remote desktop), not for seamless jumping.

Since you are using a Mac Mini and a MacBook Air, you likely already have a free feature built into your computers that does exactly what you are asking for.

The Best Solution: Universal Control (Free & Built-in)

Apple has a feature called Universal Control that allows you to use the keyboard and trackpad/mouse from your MacBook Air to control your Mac Mini (and vice versa) simply by pushing the cursor to the edge of the screen.

How to set it up:

  1. Sign In: Ensure both Macs are signed into the same iCloud account (Apple ID) with Two-Factor Authentication enabled.
  2. Enable Connectivity: Turn on Wi-Fi and Bluetooth on both Macs and keep them near each other.
  3. Turn it On:
    • Go to System Settings > Displays.
    • Click the Advanced... button.
    • Toggle on "Allow your pointer and keyboard to move between any nearby Mac or iPad."
  4. How to use it: Just push your mouse cursor to the edge of your screen (e.g., the right side of your laptop screen) and keep pushing. It will "pop" onto the Mac Mini's monitor. Your keyboard will automatically type on whichever screen your mouse is currently on.

Alternative: Logitech Flow (If you have Logitech hardware)

If you prefer third-party hardware or Universal Control isn't working for you, you can use a mouse and keyboard that supports Logitech Flow.

  • Requirements: A compatible Logitech mouse (like the MX Master series) and keyboard.
  • How it works: You install the Logi Options+ software on both computers. Similar to Universal Control, moving the mouse to the edge of the screen switches the mouse and the keyboard to the other computer automatically.

Summary

  • For "Jumping": Use Universal Control (Built-in) or Logitech Flow (Requires specific hardware).
  • For "Button Pressing": You could use a standard USB Switch (where you press a physical button to swap the USB connection of your mouse/keyboard), but this does not allow the "jumping" cursor feature you requested.

turns.prompt_text: would that work with an MK670 Wave keyboard and mouse combo? https://www.crowdsupply.com/techxartisan/openterface-mini-kvm
turns.response_html:
Yes, that keyboard and mouse combo will work, but it functions differently than a standard KVM switch.

Here is how the Logitech MK670 Wave would interact with the Openterface Mini-KVM:

1. The Primary Method (Software Relay)

You would keep your MK670 connected to your laptop (Host) as usual.

  • How it works: You type and move your mouse on your laptop. The Openterface app on your laptop captures those inputs and sends them to the "Target" computer (e.g., your Mac Mini) via the USB cable.
  • Why it works: The Mini-KVM emulates a generic keyboard and mouse, so it doesn't matter what brand of physical keyboard you use. As long as your laptop recognizes the MK670, the KVM can send its signals to the other computer.

2. The Direct Method (USB Passthrough)

You can plug the Logitech USB receiver directly into the Switchable USB-A Port on the Openterface device itself.

  • How it works: This port can be toggled to connect directly to the "Target" computer.
  • Result: The Target computer would see the Logitech receiver as if it were plugged directly into it. This is useful if you want to bypass your laptop entirely for input, but it means your laptop loses access to the keyboard until you toggle it back.

Summary: The MK670 works perfectly because the Openterface Mini-KVM uses standard HID (Human Interface Device) emulation, making it compatible with virtually any keyboard or mouse your computer can use.
